analysis.one_liner: Bans cruise ships from dumping sewage and wastewater in U.S. coastal waters and sets treatment, inspection, and enforcement standards.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 48 cosponsors, including 3 Republicans, but was never taken up by the House committee that received it and died without a vote when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Cruise ships carrying millions of passengers each year discharge sewage, wastewater from sinks and showers, and oily bilge water into U.S. coastal waters under loose or poorly enforced rules. This bill would have banned those discharges inside territorial waters, set strict treatment and testing limits for any discharge farther out, required unannounced Coast Guard inspections and onboard observers, and let citizens sue violators. It also would have charged cruise ships a fee of up to $10 per passenger to pay for the enforcement program.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live on, visit, or make a living from the coasts: swimmers, beachgoers, fishermen, and coastal tourism businesses. The bill's findings note that cruise sewage nutrients can kill coral reefs and increase pathogens in the water, and that existing law did not adequately control, monitor, or enforce cruise ship discharges [S3]. Coast Guard and EPA enforcement would be funded by fees on the cruise vessels themselves, not taxpayers [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits cruise vessels entering U.S. ports from discharging sewage, graywater, or bilge water into U.S. waters, with exceptions only beyond the territorial sea if the discharge meets effluent limits and management standards [S2].

Requires the Coast Guard and EPA to set effluent limits — at minimum, strict fecal coliform and chlorine standards — and requires announced and unannounced inspections, discharge logbooks, and at least one unannounced inspection of every cruise vessel each year [S2].

Establishes civil and criminal penalties for violations, including felonies for knowingly violating the discharge rules or falsifying monitoring records, and lets citizens sue violators or sue the agencies if they fail to enforce [S2].
Protects cruise ship employees from being fired for reporting violations or testifying in enforcement proceedings, with reinstatement and back pay ordered by the Labor Department [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cruise ship owners and operators, who would bear the cost of advanced treatment systems, inspections, monitoring equipment, discharge logbooks, penalties for violations, and a fee of up to $10 per paying passenger to fund the enforcement program [S2]. Some of that cost would likely be passed to cruise passengers through ticket prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cruise ship operators and their passengers

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose significant compliance costs on the cruise industry — advanced treatment systems, mandatory inspections, real-time monitoring technology, and a per-passenger fee — costs that would largely flow to consumers through higher ticket prices [S2].

The bill gives special compliance deadlines to Alaskan cruise vessels that already have advanced treatment systems certified by Alaska, shielding them from most requirements for up to 15 years — an exception that weakens the national standard in one of the busiest cruise regions [S2].
It applies only to passenger vessels carrying at least 250 passengers with sleeping facilities, so smaller vessels and government ships would not be covered [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and economic value of clean coastal waters — for beaches, fisheries, coral reefs, and the coastal tourism that depends on them — is broad and lasting, while the compliance costs fall on a small, highly profitable industry and its customers. The bill is real regulation with real teeth: inspections, felony penalties, citizen suits, and industry-funded enforcement. Its main design flaws are the long Alaskan carve-out and the narrow definition of covered vessels, but on balance the public benefit clearly outweighs the cost to the industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and two of its subcommittees the day after introduction, and it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Farr (D-CA) introduced the Clean Cruise Ship Act of 2005 on April 14, 2005, joined by 25 original cosponsors [S1].

It was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, then to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation and the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment [S5].
The bill attracted 48 cosponsors, 45 Democrats and 3 Republicans [S4].
No further action was recorded; the bill never left committee and received no vote in either chamber before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cruise operators came out ahead: they avoided new discharge limits, mandatory unannounced inspections, monitoring requirements, penalties, and a fee of up to $10 per passenger. Coastal waters remained governed by the weaker pre-existing rules the bill's findings called inadequate [S3].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cruise operators, who faced no new rules

for.name: Rep. Sam Farr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 25 original cosponsors

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Don Young (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — during the two years remaining in the Congress

against.name: Cruise Lines International Association
against.role: Industry trade group for major cruise lines
against.what_they_did: Opposed national cruise ship discharge standards of the kind this bill proposed, favoring voluntary programs and state-by-state arrangements

sides.party_line_note: Nearly all of the bill's 48 cosponsors were Democrats (45 of 48, with 3 Republicans), and the committee that declined to act on it was chaired by a Republican from Alaska, the state with a large cruise industry [S4].

industries.note: The bill would ban discharges in coastal waters, require treatment systems and unannounced inspections, impose penalties including felony liability for knowing violations, and charge up to $10 per passenger to fund enforcement [S2]. Its compliance costs are the direct flip side of the cleaner water the public would get.

industries.industry: Marine sanitation and pollution-monitoring equipment makers
industries.note: The bill mandates advanced treatment and requires a pilot program to develop and commercialize real-time discharge-monitoring technology, tested on at least 10% of cruise vessels, with industry partners covering at least 20% of project costs [S3].
The bill's findings link cruise sewage to coral reef damage and elevated pathogens in coastal waters, which threaten the beaches, reefs, and fisheries these businesses depend on [S3].
